title: Every day is a good day
word: Every day is a good day
hook: Yunmen asks about the days after the fifteenth, and answers himself: every day is a good day (Blue Cliff Record 6)
carry: every day is a good day

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanquan's cat, a hard one, and your line, sandals on the head. Did you catch a quarrel upside down? Day two hundred eighty-six, and something gentler.

Some days are plainly good. The test came back clear. The kids laughed at dinner. Someone you love said the thing you needed to hear. And some days are not. The car won't start. The news is bad. You say the wrong thing and lie awake replaying it. If someone told you on one of those days, every day is a good day, you might want to throw something at them. And yet in Japan those exact words hang on scrolls in tea rooms and homes, brushed in bold black ink. They come from a Zen teacher who asked his monks a question no one could answer.
screen: `THE TEST CAME BACK CLEAR.` → `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `WORDS ON A SCROLL IN A TEA ROOM.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Yunmen, who lived in southern China in the tenth century and was famous for answers so short they felt like a slap of cold water. The Blue Cliff Record, in case six, says he told his monks: I'm not asking you about the days before the fifteenth. Tell me something about the days after the fifteenth. Nobody said a word. So Yunmen answered for them: every day is a good day. The fifteenth is the middle of the lunar month, the night of the full moon. Teachers often read it as a picture. Before the fifteenth is the time of practice and searching. After the fifteenth is life after the moon is full, after insight. What's it like then? Every day is a good day. Now here's what it doesn't mean. It doesn't mean every day is pleasant, or that you should paste a smile over grief. The good in Yunmen's line isn't the opposite of bad. It's more like: this day, exactly as it comes, is the one you get to live, and there's no better one waiting somewhere else. A day of loss is still a day of your life, and it can be met completely. Zen teachers often point out that a monk who says every day is a good day still weeps at a funeral. He just doesn't throw the day away. It's close to yesterday's upside-down sandals and to the washed bowl. Stop waiting for the real day. This is it.
screen: `YUNMEN'S QUESTION.` · `AFTER THE FIFTEENTH.` · `NOT EVERY DAY IS PLEASANT.` · `NO BETTER DAY WAITING.` · then, large: `EVERY DAY IS A GOOD DAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Look back over today so far, the whole thing, not just the highlights. The alarm. The first thing you ate. The small annoyance. The small kindness. Without grading any of it, let it all be today. Then look for one good thing hiding in it, even a tiny one: warm water, a sentence someone said, the fact that you're breathing now. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
Every day is a good day. Yunmen's answer to his own question: not that every day is pleasant, but that this day is the one to live.
screen: `EVERY DAY IS A GOOD DAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every day is a good day. Tonight, before sleep, name one good thing today held, especially if it was a hard one. Day two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Yunmen's words are among the most popular Zen phrases in Japan, where they're often brushed as calligraphy and hung in tea rooms; teachers use the case to point to meeting each day fully rather than judging it.

original.note: Chinese rì rì shì hǎo rì; in Japanese, nichi nichi kore kōjitsu: every day is a good day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful slogan for looking on the bright side.
what it means: this day, exactly as it comes, is the one to live fully.
what a scholar hears: the 'fifteenth' is the full moon of the lunar month; Yunmen founded one of the five houses of Chan, and his line is case six of the Blue Cliff Record.

notes: The 'before/after the fifteenth' as practice/after insight is a common reading, not stated in the case; presented as 'teachers often read it'.
'A monk who says every day is a good day still weeps at a funeral' is a general teacher's point, not a quotation; Keeper may trim.
Yunmen Wenyan (864–949); Yunmen as one of the five houses of Chan: confirm.
